Experimental and Simulation of Compression after Impact 
(CAI) Tests for Thermoplastic Composite Materials
M. M. Shahzamanian1,2 · Sydney Houck1,3 · Li Ai2 · Md Mushfiqur Rahman Fahim3 · 
Sourav Banerjee3 · Wout De Backer1,3 · Paul Ziehl1,2
Applied Composite Materials (2025) 32:2395–2430
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10443-025-10368-8
Abstract
Damage caused by low velocity impacts in composite materials may go undetected, result­
ing in significant damage being unnoticeable. This phenomenon has been studied using 
experiments and simulations on a typical composite material, Toray T1225 LM-PAEK UD 
Tape, following impacts with varying energy levels. To the authors’ knowledge, there is a 
lack of information on thermoplastics and compression after impact (CAI) in the publicly 
available literature, and there have been insufficient results and discussions regarding CAI 
tests on thermoplastic composite materials at the relatively high levels of impact used, 
especially with the rise in the use of thermoplastic materials for the advanced air mobil­
ity market. This paper provides experimentally gathered data and describes a numerical 
approach to aid in the prediction of CAI strength for materials that are of interest to the 
advanced air mobility market. It has been observed that compressive strength decreases 
significantly even for a range of damage growth and levels of impact energy. This decrease 
occurs with damage (dent depth) below 0.1 inches (2.54 mm (mm)) and impact energy 
well below 30 Joules, even though the resulting damage may be barely visible. Finite ele­
ment (FE) simulation was carried out to better understand the development and growth 
of damage in the composite material during the CAI tests. There exist a few restrictions 
to implement a high-fidelity CAI model. Dynamic instability resulting from the impact 
must be suppressed during compression by employing mass scaling with a significantly 
low target time increment. The complexity of problems and need for detail make current 
models take days to run, even on high performance computing (HPC) clusters. Therefore, 
a “simplified” CAI test was implemented in ABAQUS using symmetric boundary condi­
tions (BCs), even when the composite had +/-45° plies and lacked full symmetry. This 
approach allowed testing different quarters of the full CAI specimen to identify which 
one showed the most damage and lowest compressive strength. The design ultimate load 
(DUL) has been selected based on the experimental and simulation results, considering a 
safety factor suitable for the ranges of static loadings when barely visible impact damage 
(BVID) occurs.
Keywords  Composite materials · Compression after impact (CAI) · Finite element

1  Introduction
Carbon fibers are less dense and less expensive to produce than boron, which makes it a pop­
ular choice for aerospace structures that need greater specific strength (strength/density) and 
specific moduli (strength/modulus) [1]. Therefore, a high-strength laminate made of carbon 
fiber-reinforced epoxy provides superior specific strength and specific modulus compared 
to traditional materials such as titanium, steel, or aluminum. This is the primary reason why 
carbon fiber reinforced plastic (CFRP) materials are popular in the aircraft industry [2]. 
On the contrary, a unidirectional laminate is anisotropic and only demonstrates excellent 
tensile strength in the direction of the fiber. To decrease the anisotropy of a fiber-reinforced 
laminate and enhance its strength in different directions fibers are typically arranged in 
various configurations of 0º, 90º, and +/−45º orientations [3], which also improves damage 
tolerance.
Low-velocity impact is a critical design case for CFRP laminates because it significantly 
reduces residual mechanical properties [4, 5]. CFRP laminates are prone to matrix cracking 
and delamination failure as a result of impact events [6] and this is more true for those made 
with unidirectional tapes. The dissipation of impact energy within the laminate results in 
matrix cracking and the force of the object causes the laminate to bend during the impact 
event. This results in inter-laminar shear forces that lead to delamination of plies [3]. The 
reinforcing fibers lack support when the matrix material fails near the surfaces. This causes 
the material to be unable to withstand the transverse force from the impacting object, ulti­
mately leading to fiber breakage. Dents caused by crushing or material failure will appear 
on the top surface or layers [7]. Visual inspection, as a non-destructive testing (NDT) tech­
nique, is used to correlate the probability of detecting cracks in metallic aircraft structures 
to their size. On the contrary, surface flaws caused by impacts on composite materials could 
go undetected, leading to unnoticed significant damage [2]. Subsurface delamination and 
a three-dimensional (3D) surface indentation are generated by impacting an object onto a 
CFRP material [8]. However, only surface indentation is visible and the delamination within 
the subsurface and cracks in the material are not visible.
It is generally accepted that the extent of impact damage on a laminate material largely 
depends on its thickness [9]. For example, the impact results leading to delamination are 
three times greater in a laminate with 16 plies compared to a laminate with 10 plies [8]. A 
thin laminate, such as a 2 mm thick laminate, will bend over a long span when impacted and 
is at risk of failure either through bending or by penetration. On the contrary, thick lami­
nates commonly used in aerospace applications [10], including 15, 30, or 60 plies, are more 
prone to delamination failure [6, 11]. Results show that impacts larger than 140 Joules, with 
a diameter of 20 mm, cause dents about 2.5 mm deep on a 7 mm laminate [8]. In contrast, 
fewer than 20 Joules are required for the 20 mm impactor to create the same dent depth on a 
1.89 mm laminate. It can be concluded that thick laminates will show less indentation under 
the same impact conditions. However, there may be substantial delamination damage under 
the indented surface that is not visible to the naked eye.
Barely visible impact damage (BVID) refers to a specified threshold for permanent 
indentations that signifies the smallest size of damage that can be reliably identified through 
visual examination [12, 13]. Below BVID, the structure is expected to handle the maximum 
loads, while above BVID, it becomes essential to apply limit loads [14]. Figure 1(a) pres­
ents a schematic illustration that depicts how BVID is determined in relation to the residual

All engineering components are susceptible to low-velocity impact incidents that can 
occur during installation, servicing, and maintenance activities. Although the reasons for 
these events can vary, components constructed from laminated composite materials com­
monly experience delamination and transverse matrix cracking as a consequence. Both 
types of damage considerably diminish the post-impact performance, particularly affect­
ing the compressive strength after the impact occurs [15–18]. Damage resistance can be 
assessed through the implementation of drop-weight impact tests and CAI tests [19]. CAI 
tests were performed in two phases: the first phase involved inducing localized damage 
through a drop-weight impact, and the second phase focused on evaluating the residual 
compressive strength of the laminate [20, 21]. Typically, the compression test should be 
performed several days after the impact to permit stress relaxation to occur. For example, 
Piotr Bajurko [19] carried out the compression test seven days after the impact.
FEM is one method for simulating impact tests [22]. The FE method is an effective 
approach for simulating both low-velocity impact tests [23, 24] and CAI tests [25–27]. 
Damage modeling for composites with the FEM can be executed by employing either 
stress-based or strain-based failure criteria. Polynomial failure criteria, such as the Tsai-Wu 
and Tsai-Hill criteria, are commonly employed to establish the failure boundary of multidi­
rectional laminates subjected to multi-axial loading. These criteria are based on equivalent 
stress or strain assessments [28]. Hashin developed a failure criterion for unidirectional 
composites that individually addresses four different failure modes: fiber damage in ten­
sion, fiber damage in compression, and matrix failure under both tensile and compressive 
loadings [29, 30]. The Hashin damage criterion has been employed by various researchers 
to predict damage within FEMs for composite materials [31–33].
The transition from thermoset to thermoplastic composites is essential to achieve the high 
production rates needed for urban air mobility (UAM) vehicles [34]. While the manufactur­
ing rate of thermoset composites can be enhanced through the use of parallel production 
lines due to their lengthy curing processes, thermoplastic composites benefit from a much 
shorter consolidation cycle. This allows for increased manufacturing rates without requir­
ing multiple production lines. Additionally, thermoplastics offer the advantage of being able 
to be remelted and reconsolidated without adversely affecting their mechanical properties 
[34]. In this study, experiments along with FE modeling were performed for CAI testing 
to understand the progression of damage in a typical thermoplastic composite material. To

2  Experimental Methodology
2.1  Fabrication of Composite Materials
The samples were made by hand layup with Toray T1225 LM-PAEK UD Tape with a stack­
ing sequence of [+ 45/0/−45/90]4S (32 plies). Unidirectional tape was used, and the volume 
fraction of the fiber was ~ 65%. The plies of material were cut at specified angles for the 
different orientations, based on the stacking sequence, at the desired size of 24 inches by 24 
inches (609.6 mm by 609.6 mm). Each of the layers was tacked together using a soldering 
iron. Figure 2 shows one of the panels completed with hand layup. A vacuum bag was then 
created to cure the panel using the autoclave. The TC1225 was processed around 100–120 
psi (0.689–0.827 MPa), and 695 F (368 C). Figure 3 shows the bagging sequence and mate­
rials used for the vacuum bag, as well as a finished vacuum bag with the panel. Once the 
panel was consolidated with the autoclave, a wet saw was used to cut the panel into 4 inches 
by 6 inches (101.6 mm by 152.4 mm) samples that could be used for impact testing. The 
thickness of the composite materials is 4.6 mm +/- 0.1 mm.
2.2  Impact Test
Each of the 4 inches by 6 inches samples were impacted using a drop weight method, 
according to ASTM 7136. As seen in Fig. 4 there were four clamps holding the panels in 
place during the impact. The samples were inserted in the impact tower following the ori­
entation also shown in Fig. 4. The impact energies ranged from 0 Joules to 60 Joules. These 
energy levels were accomplished by adjusting the height and weight of the impact tower, 
which can be changed for any energy level. To record the experimental energy level of the 
impacts, a photogate was used to measure the velocity of the impactor right before it reaches 
the plate. This velocity value was used to calculate the impact energy.
2.3  Compression Test
After the samples were impacted each panel was compression tested. Figure 5 illustrates the 
fixture and set up for the compression test. The side surfaces as well as end surface of the 
material have been clamped and the top assembly was used to apply compressive loading.

3  Finite Element (FE) Simulation
This section explains the FE modeling of the CAI test on composite materials. First, it 
provides a description of the simulation of the composite materials in ABAQUS. Then, a 
detailed description of the impact testing simulation is provided. Finally, the compression 
test is explained to demonstrate the compressive strength of a material after impact testing.
3.1  Damage Model of Composite Material
In this study, the in-built Hashin damage model [29, 30] in ABAQUS is utilized as an appro­
priate failure criterion to predict damage modes and effective damage evolution model to 
describe the composite stiffness degradation.

3.3  Simulation of Composite Materials
There are several methods for simulating composite materials in ABAQUS. This study 
focused on simulating a 3D structure with multiple plies. The effective properties of the 
various layers were calculated and taken into account for the 3D structure. The 3D struc­
ture was meshed using continuum shell elements with fewer elements than the number of 
plies in this study to expedite the computation. However, it is important to note that a mesh 
sensitivity analysis was conducted to determine the smallest number of elements needed for 
the simulation.
Composite materials consist of layers with various orientations, including +/−45°, which 
makes the overall layup asymmetric. As a result, symmetric boundary conditions (BCs) are 
generally not applicable. However, in this study, symmetric BCs were applied to simplify 
the model and reduce computational time. A detailed discussion of the justification and 
implications of this approach will be provided in the following sub-section.
Composite layups were used to model the composites, including 32 plies with the ply 
sequence [+ 45/0/−45/90]4 S in ABAQUS. The elasticity, considering the type of lamina, 
was used to incorporate the effect of anisotropy in the elastic response of composites. Table 
1 presents the elastic properties at various orientations [39]. The built-in Hashin damage 
criterion [29, 30] was utilized, and the maximum values of strength at various orientations 
are presented in Table 2. Damage evolution is accounted for as damage begins when stress

3.4  Simulation of Impact Test
In the impact testing simulation in ABAQUS, discrete rigid bodies were used for the sam­
ple holder, impactor, and support fixture. Surface-to-surface contact interactions were used 
between the sample and the parts, including the impactor, holder, and sample support. The 
simulated impact test is shown in Fig. 7. The impact test was conducted to investigate the 
effect of the friction coefficient between the composite materials, the holder, and the impac­
tor. It was found that the friction coefficient has a negligible effect on the reaction force 
applied to the impactor when the mesh is fine enough. Therefore, we assumed that the fric­
tion coefficient falls within a reasonable range, typically between 0.4 and 0.5. The friction 
coefficient has a significant effect when the elements are coarse, but this effect decreases as 
the element size decreases.
Coarse meshes with 4-node 3-D bilinear rigid quadrilateral (R3D4) elements for the 
sample holders and fixture were used to expedite the computation process. A fine mesh 
was used for the impactor to account for its curved shape, which can affect the simulation 
results. The velocity of the impactor was measured using a photogate located very close to 
the sample. Therefore, the impactor has been located very close to the sample at the start of 
the FE simulation, using the measured velocity as the initial velocity.
The sample holder was fixed in place during impact testing by constraining every degree 
of freedom for all nodes. An appropriate amount of pressure was applied to the support 
fixture to keep the sample tightly in contact with the sample holder during the impact. The 
impact test was conducted using ABAQUS/Explicit step without mass scaling because the 
results of the test are dependent on time and the problem is explicitly dynamic.
3.5  Simulation of Compression Test
The compression test was simulated and the boundary conditions on the samples were 
applied in a way that resembles the test taking place in experiments, as shown in Fig. 8. 
The vertical displacement (U2) at the edges was constrained because of the presence of a 
side wall in the experiment. The perpendicular displacement (U3) at points on two faces of 
the specimen very close to the edge was constrained because of the side fixtures that were 
installed. This boundary condition is not the actual one because the actual side fixtures were 
not simulated in order to reduce the number of elements and speed up the computation. 
Therefore, this boundary condition may yield engineering results. Furthermore, the degree 
of freedom for the partition at the end of the specimen were coupled on a reference point. 
The applied displacement in X direction was inserted on that reference point when the other 
degrees of freedom were constrained.

was used with the mass scaling technique to eliminate dynamic instability. The level of 
kinetic energy of the material was high at the end of the impact test. Therefore, a very low 
value of time increment, such as 1.0e-5, was used for mass scaling in the compression test 
to eliminate dynamic instability and make the test resemble a quasi-static problem. The 
ABAQUS simulations were aborted during the compression test when using a time incre­
ment greater than 1.0 e-5. The computations were rather expensive as have been reported 
elsewhere. Lin et al. [25] have stated that simulating the CAI test could take days, even 
on high performance computing (HPC) clusters. Therefore, an algorithm has been imple­
mented by Lin et al. [25] to import the calculated damage from the impact simulation to the 
compression simulation. They conducted a simulation of the compression test, considering 
the initial values of damage for each individual case. In this way, they eliminated any kinetic 
energy caused during impact simulation that has the potential to create dynamic instability. 
In addition, they have utilized a mesh paradigm to decrease the number of elements and 
implement finer elements in areas where it is necessary, such as only at the central part 
of the specimen where damage is caused by impact. It should be noted that Lin et al. [25] 
simulated the individual plies with consideration of cohesive elements between layers to 
account for the effect of delamination. However, in this study, delamination is not taken into 
consideration to expedite the computation process, and instead a 3D composite structure 
was simulated as previously described. The aim of this paper was to understand how dam­
age progresses in a composite material to help in constructing DUL. It is important to note 
that the precise progression of damage is best determined experimentally. However, it is 
noted that the damage progression observed in the FE simulation, even without considering 
delamination between layers, was similar to the experiments reported by other researchers. 
Damage initiates at 80% of displacements in CAI tests as identified by acoustic emission 
(AE) and reported by Biagini [41]. The relationship between cumulative signal strength 
(CSS) and force was analyzed for each compression test in the current study, with the find­
ings illustrated in Fig. 9. It is evident that the sharp increase in CSS did not coincide with 
the peak force for these tests as observed by Biagini [41]. Notably, in the test with an impact 
energy of 5 Joules, three distinct rises in CSS were observed, whereas all other tests showed 
only a single increase. The CSS curves presented in Fig. 9 were derived from the signal 
strengths recorded by AE sensors mounted on the specimen during the compression test. A 
detailed analysis of the AE data falls outside the scope of this study and is intended to be the 
focus of a future investigation by the authors.
Also, as will be observed, the compressive strength for different impact energies will be

experimentally and numerically as damage is almost constant until the late stage of strain­

3.7  A Simplified CAI Model Using Symmetric BCs
Although the CAI test geometry is symmetric, the presence of +/−45 plies in composite 
materials introduces asymmetry. As a result, symmetric boundary conditions cannot be used 
to model just a quarter or half of the specimen. The matrix compressive damage distribution 
after impact across the full specimen resembles an angled dumbbell shape (see Fig. 10). The 
majority of surface matrix compressive damage is concentrated in two diagonally opposite 
quarters, while the other two diagonal quarters experience significantly less matrix compres­
sive damage. The diagonal quarters after impact that undergo greater matrix compressive 
damage tend to experience less fiber tensile damage, whereas the quarters with higher fiber 
tensile damage show less matrix compressive damage. A careful examination of the stress 
and damage distribution in the simulated full specimen of the CAI test reveals that, despite 
the asymmetry in local stress and damage patterns, the overall magnitude of stress and dam­

4  Results and Discussion
The FE simulation for the quarter specimen with ply sequence [+ 45,0,−45,90]4S was con­
ducted, and the results are presented in this section along with discussion. Based on our lat­
est discussion, the quarter specimen with ply sequence [+ 45,0,−45,90]4S predicts the lowest 
compressive strength compared to [−45,0,45,90]4S and it is comparable to half specimen. 
First, the results of the impact testing are presented and discussed. Then, the results of the 
compression test after the impact are presented. Finally, the research investigated the pro­
gression of damage during impact and compression. Furthermore, the effect of damage on 
the residual compressive strength is presented and discussed to provide a suitable approach 
for improving the design of composite materials and the selection of DUL.

4.1  Simulation of Impact Testing
The impactor hits the composite material as it is being held tightly by the sample holder 
and the support fixture. First, the kinetic energies of the whole system given by ABAQUS 
for every simulation have been tested and presented in Fig. 13. It has been observed that 
ABAQUS can accurately run simulations with the correct levels of kinetic energy when the 
simulations are set based on the parameters set up in experiments. These parameters include 
the mass of the impactor, the initial velocity of the impactor, and the height of the impactor. 
As demonstrated in Fig. 13, the higher the impact energy, the higher the value of kinetic 
energy at the beginning, because the impactor has a higher initial velocity. Then, the kinetic 
energy reaches zero when the impactor returns, and its velocity is zero at that moment. 
Finally, the kinetic energy increases and then settles at a value that is lower than the initial 
kinetic energy. As shown in Fig. 13, the time when the impactor returns is higher for higher 
values of impact energies as expected.
The damage areas created due to impact at the center of the specimen for various impact 
energies were presented and compared to the damage zone obtained experimentally using 
the C-Scan technique. The damage diameter was measured for both cases, the experiment 
and ABAQUS, and the error percentages were then presented. As illustrated and discussed 
in Fig. 10, two distinct damage patterns appear in the two adjoining quarters of the speci­
men; however, the major and minor diameters of the damage distributions are nearly the 
same. Figure 14 shows comparisons of the damage at various impact energy levels. For 
such and analysis, we considered the damage distribution for the quarter specimen with ply 
sequence [+ 45/0/−45/90]4S that predicts the lowest compressive strength. It can be deduced 
that the Hashin damage values presented by Ref [40]. predict rather accurate results under 
quasi-static loading and low impact energy. The error percentage for the low values of 
impact energy is very low. However, the error percentage increases with an increase in 
impact energy. Overall, it is observed that the comparison of the shapes in damage zones 
and the error percentages is in an appropriate order for numerically estimating the damage 
zone up to 60 joules due to the interactions of many parameters and factors in the simulation 
process and limitations in computation.

further strain is required for a few tests, especially for the one with an impact energy of 60

be emphasized that the objective of this study is to present the results before fracture, spe­
cifically when the maximum force value is reached. The scattering results at fracture have 
no influence on the results presented in this paper.

5  Discussion on the Selection of Design Ultimate Load (DUL) Assisted 
by the Simulated Results
As mentioned previously, composite materials are being used as replacements for traditional 
materials in aircraft components due to their high strength-to-density ratio [2]. Additionally, 
it is essential to control the applied load on the composite materials throughout the duration 
of the flight. In this study, the focus has been on the static applied load and primarily the 
effect of impact on compressive strength. It is very important to understand the threshold 
for visibility of damage that occurs during impact tests. As stated in MIL-HDBK-17 [9], 
the visibility cut-off for composite materials is the depth of damage at 0.1 inches when the 
energy is below 140 Joules [2]. This amount of energy is the highest level of impact damage 
that is likely to occur to a composite aircraft structure before the damage propagates from 
being barely visible (0.1 inches) to easily detectable damage. Figure 21(a) shows a diagram 
illustrating visibility and energy cut-offs, as well as experimental findings on the depth of 
damage at different impact energies for the composite materials analyzed in this study. As 
shown in Fig. 21(a), the depth of damage increases with higher impact energy, and visibility 
increases as expected. For nearly half of the experiments conducted in this study involving 
lower impact energies, there is very little visible damage. Therefore, the focus must be on 
those tests with respect to the growth of damage, as there is little indication of damage. 
Compressive strength against dent depth has been presented in Fig. 21(b). It has been noted 
that the compressive strengths are the lowest for three tests, while there is no visible damage 
growth according to the visibility cut-off criterion. These three tests correspond to an impact 
energy of 30 Joules. Therefore, in this study, the design ultimate load (DUL) capability for 
FAR 25.305 analysis is determined based on the selection criterion for BVID as discussed 
and shown in Fig. 1(a). The compressive strength corresponding to the test with an impact 
energy of 30 Joules has been selected as the lowest DUL. As shown in Fig. 22, compressive 
strength decreases with a higher impact energy. However, the damage grows as the impact 
energy increases. Figure 22 clearly shows that damage for tests lower than impact energy of 
30 Joules is not visible, but the compressive strength is high enough to withstand additional 
loads on the material. On the other hand, the compressive strengths for the tests with impact 
energies greater than 30 Joules are the lowest, but damage is visible, and the material can 
be replaced during the maintenance service. The most crucial tests correspond to impact 
energies around 30 Joules. In these tests, compressive strength is low, and damage is barely 
visible.
The compressive strains for each experiment have been calculated and compared to the 
impact energies (see Fig. 23). The lowest amount of strain applied that corresponds to the 
experiment with an impact energy of 30 Joules is 0.015. Therefore, this compressive strain 
could be considered as the specifically chosen BVID that determines the design ultimate 
load (DUL) capability for FAR 25.305 analysis [9]. The DUL is defined as the visibility 
cut-off based on the definition of 0.1 inches damage depth as shown in Fig. 1(a). Based on 
the description and the information shown in Fig. 1(b), the safety factor of 1.5 for the DUL 
should be considered for the range of impact tests near the BVID. Therefore, the compres­
sive strain with a DUL, considering the safety factor, would be 0.01. The DUL thresholds 
with and without consideration of a safety factor have been added to Fig. 23.

any clear indication, indicating that it is necessary to consider the DUL with a safety factor 
of 1.5 for tests involving impact energies of around 30 Joules.
6  Conclusions
Recently, there has been a fast shift in replacing thermosets with thermoplastic composite 
materials. The current article presents the results and discussions regarding CAI tests on 
thermoplastic composite materials at relatively high levels of impact. Damage development 
in a composite material under low velocity impact and its subsequent effect on compres­
sive strength has been studied both experimentally and numerically using FE simulation. 
The numerical compressive strength was compared to the experimental results and then the 
damage growth during impact at various levels of impact energies was analyzed. The results 
show that damage during the impact increases, then the growth stops at a certain time before 
the impactor returns. The level of damage increases as the impact energy increases, which 
results in a decrease in the compressive strength of a composite material after impact. It is 
suggested that damage progression is not readily visible below a certain threshold known 
as BVID during low velocity impact. FE simulation was carried out and the level of dam­
age was measured using a simplified implemented model. Damage is nearly constant dur­
ing compression, but it increases sharply when final fracture occurs. Therefore, DUL was 
defined as the point where damage is barely visible and the compressive strength of the 
material substantially decreases due to impact. This type of load design has been deemed 
necessary based on a thorough observation of experimental results showing that the com­
pressive strength decreased after an impact with energy of 30 Joules, even though visible 
damage was barely apparent.

Abstract: Damage caused by low velocity impacts in composite materials may go undetected, result­ ing in significant damage being unnoticeable. This phenomenon has been studied using experiments and simulations on a typical composite material, Toray T1225 LM-PAEK UD Tape, following impacts with varying energy levels. To the authors’ knowledge, there is a lack of information on thermoplastics and compression after impact (CAI) in the publicly available literature, and there have been insufficient results and discussions regarding CAI tests on thermoplastic composite materials at the relatively high levels of impact used, especially with the rise in the use of thermoplastic materials for the advanced air mobil­ ity market. This paper provides experimentally gathered data and describes a numerical approach to aid in the prediction of CAI strength for materials that are of interest to the advanced air mobility market. It has been observed that compressive strength decreases significantly even for a range of damage growth and levels of impact energy. This decrease occurs with damage (dent depth) below 0.1 inches (2.54 mm (mm)) and impact energy well below 30 Joules, even though the resulting damage may be barely visible. Finite ele­ ment (FE) simulation was carried out to better understand the development and growth of damage in the composite material during the CAI tests. There exist a few restrictions to implement a high-fidelity CAI model. Dynamic instability resulting from the impact must be suppressed during compression by employing mass scaling with a significantly low target time increment. The complexity of problems and need for detail make current models take days to run, even on high performance computing (HPC) clusters. Therefore, a “simplified” CAI test was implemented in ABAQUS using symmetric boundary condi­ tions (BCs), even when the composite had +/-45° plies and lacked full symmetry. This approach allowed testing different quarters of the full CAI specimen to identify which one showed the most damage and lowest compressive strength. The design ultimate load (DUL) has been selected based on the experimental and simulation results, considering a safety factor suitable for the ranges of static loadings when barely visible impact damage (BVID) occurs.
